issues.item: Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
issues.explanation: For terrorism trauma in a 70-year-old civilian dentist, 'seeing the offender' is hard to reconcile unless the patient had direct repeated exposure to an identified perpetrator; with the rest of the profile focused on generalized danger cues (uniforms, military topics, loud sounds, exits, watching others), this item stands out as clinically implausible for the same trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid evaluation' reflects social/performance-evaluation avoidance, but no threat, trigger, or memory items involve shame, scrutiny, appearance, or performance. It does not fit the otherwise terrorism-focused hypervigilance/trauma-reminder pattern and looks like a strategy for a different symptom cluster.

vignette:
Carlos, a 70-year-old dentist who lost his wife to cancer three years ago, still runs his small practice two days a week in a suburban strip mall. The rest of his time he spends alone. The trauma that brought him to therapy happened five years earlier, on a warm September afternoon when he had taken his wife to a community festival downtown. He remembers the music, the smell of grilled corn, the way she leaned on his arm. Then he remembers the first sound - not a firecracker, he knew that immediately - and the second, and the third. He remembers the crowd surging, people falling, and the man in the dark vest who kept walking forward with the rifle. Carlos was not hit. He pulled his wife behind a concrete planter and covered her with his body until the shooting stopped. Nine people died. Twenty-three were wounded. He has never told anyone the thought that came to him in that moment, pinned under the weight of his own uselessness: I should have done something. I should have run toward him instead of hiding.

That thought has not left him. For five years, Carlos has revisited the moment of decision - that split second when he chose to protect his wife rather than intervene - and each time he arrives at the same verdict. He blames himself for not acting, even though he knows, intellectually, that he would likely have been killed. The rumination has a specific rhythm: a trigger will surface, and then the replay begins, and then the self-criticism, and then the surge of heat in his chest that forces him to stop whatever he is doing. When the memory returns in full, it arrives across all his senses at once: the pop-pop-pop of the rifle, the smell of the man's sweat as he passed within ten feet, the weight of his wife's body trembling under him, the bright blue sky that did not change. He cannot describe the event in words without the sentences breaking apart. In session, he often stops mid-sentence and shakes his head. "I can't," he says. "It's not- I can't make it make sense."

The triggers that ambush him are everywhere. Any sound like a gunshot - a car backfiring, a door slamming, a dropped metal tray in his own dental operatory - sends his heart racing and his palms sweating. He has learned to brace himself before opening a drawer of instruments. Authority figures in uniform, especially police officers and security guards, make him feel suddenly exposed and suspicious, though he cannot explain why; his mind goes to the officers who arrived at the festival afterward, the way they shouted and pushed, the way he felt herded and helpless. Military topics on television or in conversation produce a tightness in his throat, and he will change the subject or leave the room. He has stopped watching the news entirely because he cannot tolerate the inevitable coverage of shootings or bombings, even those on the other side of the world. The news is a door he keeps closed.

He has come to carry a weapon himself - a small handgun he keeps in his car console or in a shoulder bag when he is out - because the idea of being unarmed again feels intolerable. He tells himself it is practical, that it gives him options, but he also knows he checks the bag several times a day to make sure the gun is still there. When he walks into any building, his eyes go immediately to the exits. He notes the number of doors, the placement of windows, the thickness of walls. In his dental office he has rearranged his chair so that he faces the door, and he watches every person who enters for signs of threat - the way they hold their hands, the direction of their gaze, the shape of a bulge under a jacket. He is always scanning.

The avoidance has cost him. He stopped attending the community center where he used to play dominoes with other retired men; too many loud voices and sudden movements. His daughter, who lives two hours away, calls more often now because his responses to her invitations have become vague and deflecting. He says he is busy, or tired, or that he needs to stay near home because of the practice. The practice itself is shrinking; his remaining patients are long-standing ones who tolerate his occasional flinch when they walk in unannounced. He has not made a new patient appointment in months.

What brought Carlos to therapy was not a crisis, but an accumulation. He found himself, one Tuesday morning, sitting in his car in his own driveway for thirty minutes, unable to turn the key in the ignition because he thought he heard a sound like a firecracker three blocks away. He knew it was irrational. He also knew he could not make himself move. That evening, he called his daughter and told her, for the first time, that he thought something was wrong with his mind. She found him a therapist who specialized in trauma. He came to the first session with his hands folded tightly in his lap, and said, almost in a whisper, "I need to stop living like this. But I don't know how to be anywhere else."
